body.statement:
For fixed \(d,m,G\), uniformly over \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{reg}}(d,m,G;\gamma,L,d_{\min},d_{\max},\kappa)\), the vector
\[
 \sqrt n\,\operatorname{vec}_{s}\!\left(\widehat M_0-M_0,\widehat M_1-M_1\right)
\]
converges to a centered Gaussian vector with covariance \(\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\operatorname{Cov}(g_0,g_k)\), where \(g_s=\operatorname{vec}_{s}(Y_sY_s^\top-M_0,Y_sY_{s-1}^\top-M_1)\) and \(\operatorname{vec}_{s}\) stacks the distinct lag-zero entries and all lag-one entries.  The covariance series converges absolutely and uniformly.  On the event that \(\widehat B\) is stable, substituting \((\widehat B,\widehat M_0)\) into the Gaussian Isserlis covariance series and projecting the resulting symmetric matrix onto the positive-semidefinite cone gives a uniformly consistent estimator of this long-run covariance; defining it arbitrarily off that event does not affect consistency.
body.proof_tex:
Iterating the fine-grid recursion over one observed interval gives
\[
 Y_s=BY_{s-1}+\eta_s,\qquad
 B=A^m,\qquad
 \eta_s=\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}A^r\varepsilon_{ms-r}.
\]
The innovation blocks are disjoint across \(s\), so the Gaussian-innovation assumption gives independent centered Gaussian \(\eta_s\) with
\[
 \operatorname{Var}(\eta_s)=Q=\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}A^rD(A^r)^\top.
\]
The term \(r=0\) and the innovation bounds imply \(Q\succeq d_{\min}I_d\); the entry envelope, fixed \(d,m\), and \(D\preceq d_{\max}I_d\) give a finite uniform upper bound on \(\|Q\|_{\mathrm{op}}\).

Because \(A\) is lower triangular and \(\max_i|A_{ii}|\le1-\gamma\), the diagonal of \(B\) is bounded by \(\rho_0=(1-\gamma)^m<1\).  Expanding powers of a fixed-dimensional triangular matrix shows that each entry of \(B^k\) is bounded by a constant times \((k+1)^{d-1}\rho_0^{\max(k-d+1,0)}\), uniformly under the entry envelope.  Choosing any \(\rho\in(\rho_0,1)\) absorbs the polynomial factor, and hence there is a finite \(C\), depending only on the displayed class constants, such that
\[
 \sup_{(A,D)}\|B^k\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le C\rho^k,\qquad k\ge0.
\]
Stationarity now yields
\[
 M_0=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}B^jQ(B^j)^\top,\qquad
 M_1=BM_0.
\]
Consequently \(M_0\succeq Q\succeq d_{\min}I_d\), \(\|M_0\|_{\mathrm{op}}\) is uniformly bounded, and the lag covariance
\[
 \Gamma_r=\mathbb E(Y_sY_{s-r}^\top)
 =B^rM_0\quad(r\ge0),\qquad \Gamma_{-r}=\Gamma_r^\top,
\]
decays uniformly geometrically.

Index a coordinate of \(g_s\) by \((a,b,\ell)\), where \(\ell\in\{0,1\}\), and write
\[
 \xi_s^{a b\ell}=Y_{s,a}Y_{s-\ell,b}-\mathbb E(Y_{s,a}Y_{s-\ell,b}).
\]
Isserlis' identity for four centered jointly Gaussian variables, obtained by summing the three pairings and cancelling the within-product pairing, gives
\[
 \operatorname{Cov}(\xi_0^{ab\ell},\xi_k^{cd\ell'})
 =\Gamma_{-k,ac}\Gamma_{-\ell-k+\ell',bd}
  +\Gamma_{\ell'-k,ad}\Gamma_{-\ell-k,bc}.
\]
The geometric bound on \(\Gamma_r\) makes the sum over \(k\in\mathbb Z\) absolutely and uniformly convergent, coordinate by coordinate.  It also shows directly that the covariance of the normalized partial sum converges uniformly to that series, because
\[
 \frac1n\sum_{s,t=1}^{n}\operatorname{Cov}(g_s,g_t)
 =\sum_{|k|<n}\left(1-\frac{|k|}{n}\right)\operatorname{Cov}(g_0,g_k),
\]
up to the harmless fixed endpoint convention in the lag-one coordinates.

It remains to establish Gaussianity rather than only covariance convergence.  Fix a real vector \(a\) of matching dimension and stack \((Y_0,\ldots,Y_n)\) into \(\mathbf Y_n\), whose block covariance matrix is \(\Sigma_n\).  The summability of \(\Gamma_r\) implies \(\sup_n\|\Sigma_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}<\infty\).  There is a symmetric block-banded matrix \(H_{n,a}\), with uniformly bounded operator norm and \(\|H_{n,a}\|_{\mathrm F}=O(\sqrt n)\), such that
\[
 a^\top n^{-1/2}\sum_{s=1}^{n}g_s
 =n^{-1/2}\{\mathbf Y_n^\top H_{n,a}\mathbf Y_n-\operatorname{tr}(H_{n,a}\Sigma_n)\}.
\]
Writing \(\mathbf Y_n=\Sigma_n^{1/2}Z_n\) with standard Gaussian \(Z_n\), put
\[
 T_{n,a}=n^{-1/2}\Sigma_n^{1/2}H_{n,a}\Sigma_n^{1/2}.
\]
Uniformly over the class, \(\|T_{n,a}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O(n^{-1/2})\) and \(\operatorname{tr}(T_{n,a}^2)=O(1)\).  For fixed real \(t\), diagonalizing \(T_{n,a}\) gives the exact characteristic function
\[
 \mathbb E\exp\{it(Z_n^\top T_{n,a}Z_n-\operatorname{tr}T_{n,a})\}
 =\exp\left\{-it\operatorname{tr}T_{n,a}-\frac12\log\det(I-2itT_{n,a})\right\}.
\]
Expanding the logarithm is valid uniformly for all sufficiently large \(n\), and the linear term cancels, leaving
\[
 -t^2\operatorname{tr}(T_{n,a}^2)+O\!\left(|t|^3\|T_{n,a}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\operatorname{tr}(T_{n,a}^2)\right)
 =-\frac{t^2}{2}a^\top\Omega a+o(1),
\]
where \(\Omega=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\operatorname{Cov}(g_0,g_k)\).  The remainder is uniform.  Taking \(a=t\) and scalar Fourier argument one gives, for every multivariate argument \(t\), uniform convergence of the joint characteristic function to \(\exp(-t^\top\Omega t/2)\).  Uniform boundedness of the second moments gives tightness.  To see directly that this implies uniform weak convergence, truncate a bounded Lipschitz test function to a common compact ball, convolve the truncation with a Gaussian kernel, use Fourier inversion and the just-proved characteristic-function convergence for the convolution, and then let the kernel variance tend to zero and the ball radius tend to infinity.  This proves the stated uniform Gaussian limit, allowing singular \(\Omega\).

Finally, the empirical moments have variance \(O(n^{-1})\) uniformly by the same covariance summability.  Since \(M_0\succeq d_{\min}I_d\), this implies
\[
 \widehat M_0\longrightarrow M_0,\qquad
 \widehat B=\widehat M_1\widehat M_0^{-1}\longrightarrow B
\]
uniformly in probability.  A fixed neighborhood of the compact set of \(B\)'s is stable and obeys a common geometric power bound, so the stable event has probability tending to one uniformly.  Substitute
\[
 \widehat\Gamma_r=\widehat B^r\widehat M_0\quad(r\ge0),\qquad
 \widehat\Gamma_{-r}=\widehat\Gamma_r^\top
\]
into the displayed Isserlis formula and sum over \(k\in\mathbb Z\).  Uniform geometric domination and continuity of each finite partial sum yield consistency by a finite-head plus uniformly small-tail argument.  Symmetrize this estimate and project it onto the closed convex cone of positive-semidefinite matrices.  Since the true long-run covariance belongs to that cone, metric projection cannot increase its Frobenius distance from the truth.  The projected estimate is therefore also uniformly consistent and always defines a Gaussian covariance.  An arbitrary definition on the vanishing-probability unstable event leaves that conclusion unchanged.
